events.title: 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre
events.subtitle: A city’s promise, a community under attack, and the lives we continue to remember
events.intro: White mob violence began in Atlanta on September 22, 1906. Newspaper allegations and the political campaign over Black voting rights contributed to attacks on Black residents and businesses.

overview.title: Before the violence: a city being built
overview.text: Black Atlantans established businesses and community institutions during segregation. White political campaigns and sensational newspaper reports targeted Black economic and political participation.

overview.title: From downtown streets to Brownsville
overview.text: Violence began downtown on September 22, 1906, and spread into Black neighborhoods. In Brownsville, police and armed residents exchanged gunfire, followed by militia intervention and arrests.

overview.title: The work of remembering
overview.text: The National Center for Civil and Human Rights documented later efforts to commemorate the massacre, including a memorial service at George Union Wilder’s South-View grave in 2006.

events.notice: The five victims below and Alonzo Franklin Herndon offer different connections to this history. Herndon survived; his business was attacked. The visual archive shows the surrounding city and community, while each profile explains the evidence for its South-View connection.

timeline.title: Violence begins downtown
timeline.text: Unsubstantiated newspaper allegations helped gather white mobs. Attacks spread through downtown streets, public transportation, and Black businesses, including Herndon’s barbershop.

timeline.title: Families and neighborhoods under threat
timeline.text: Black residents defended their homes as violence continued. Police raided Brownsville on September 24; militia then arrested more than 250 Black men.

timeline.title: A century of remembrance
timeline.text: Centennial commemorations began with a funeral motorcade and a memorial service at George Wilder’s grave in South-View, making the cemetery a place of public acknowledgment.

timeline.title: Names returned to the record
timeline.text: Museum researchers announced confirmation of Marshall Carter and Stinson Ferguson as victims. Anniversary events and a new documentary brought this continuing work to wider audiences.

overview.title: An investigation is not the whole story
overview.text: Wayne Williams was convicted of murdering Jimmy Ray Payne and Nathaniel Cater, both adults. The FBI reported that investigators linked Williams to additional deaths. Those investigative conclusions were separate from the convictions.

overview.title: Remembrance in the city
overview.text: Atlanta’s Children’s Eternal Flame Memorial was dedicated at City Hall in June 2023. Its curved wall, names, and gathering space honor the lives lost and the families who carried their memory forward. South-View’s graves and the city memorial offer different places for the same enduring act: remembering each person by name.

events.notice: This chapter brings together young victims remembered at South-View and educators who provide broader context about children’s rights and opportunity. The educators are not presented as victims or as participants in the murder investigations.

timeline.title: The first losses
timeline.text: Milton Harvey and Yusuf Bell disappeared in Atlanta. Their names were included in the AJC’s victim gallery.

timeline.title: A city searching for answers
timeline.text: The investigation expanded as more young people disappeared. Federal investigators worked alongside local authorities; families continued to seek answers about their own children.

timeline.title: Two adult-murder convictions
timeline.text: Williams was convicted of murdering Payne and Cater on February 27, 1982. Investigators’ conclusions about other deaths were separate from those convictions.

timeline.title: A lasting public memorial
timeline.text: The Eternal Flame Memorial on Atlanta’s City Hall grounds created a public place to honor the victims and acknowledge those who helped with searches, recovery, and healing.

overview.title: Building power before the headlines
overview.text: John Wesley Dobbs founded voting organizations in Atlanta and encouraged Black residents to register to vote.

overview.title: Many routes toward equality
overview.text: Horace Mann Bond conducted historical research for the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund. His work contributed to the arguments presented in Brown v. Board of Education.

timeline.title: Organizing voters in Atlanta
timeline.text: Dobbs and A. T. Walden cofounded the Atlanta Negro Voters League, helping Black Atlantans organize political influence.

timeline.title: Challenging school segregation
timeline.text: Brown v. Board of Education rejected segregation in public schools. Horace Mann Bond’s historical research contributed to the NAACP legal team’s arguments.

timeline.title: Student action in public spaces
timeline.text: Atlanta sit-ins and the Freedom Rides challenged segregation through direct action. Ruby Doris Smith Robinson participated in both, joining personal courage with collective organizing.

timeline.title: Marchers attacked in Selma
timeline.text: John Robert Lewis and other voting-rights marchers were attacked by state troopers after crossing the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama.

alonzoherndon.name: Alonzo Franklin Herndon
alonzoherndon.intro: Alonzo Franklin Herndon was a barber, property owner, and insurance-company founder in Atlanta. Born into slavery, he built businesses that employed Black Atlantans and provided insurance to Black families. His career connected skilled work with the development of Black institutions. He also supported schools, charitable organizations, and national efforts to challenge racial exclusion.

chapters.title: From slavery to barbering
chapters.text: Herndon was born in Walton County, Georgia, on June 26, 1858. After emancipation, his family worked as sharecroppers. He left Social Circle in 1878, learned barbering, and opened a shop in Jonesboro. The New Georgia Encyclopedia dates his arrival in Atlanta to early 1883, while the Atlanta History Center’s photograph record gives 1882. Those institutional accounts differ on the year of the move.

chapters.title: An Atlanta workplace
chapters.text: The Atlanta History Center preserved a photograph of Herndon’s Atlanta barbershop taken in 1903. Its catalog identified the business as A. F. Herndon’s Tonsorial Palace and described an interior on Peachtree Street. The image showed barber chairs, mirrors, and the fittings of a workplace that served white patrons under segregation. The catalog connected that business with Herndon’s later property ownership and insurance enterprise. It provided a view of the work and physical setting behind his business career.

chapters.title: Insurance and community organizations
chapters.text: In 1905, Herndon bought a mutual aid association and incorporated the Atlanta Mutual Insurance Association. The firm became Atlanta Life Insurance Company in 1922. He also attended the founding meeting of the Niagara Movement in 1905. During the Atlanta Race Massacre, white mobs smashed his barbershop windows after he had gone home. He survived the attacks and continued his business work. His insurance company expanded into other states, while he supported Black schools and charitable organizations. His son, Norris, later continued the family’s insurance work. Herndon participated in national Black business and political organizations as well as local enterprises. His business career continued until his death in Atlanta in 1927.

alonzoherndon.note: The New Georgia Encyclopedia gives early 1883 for Herndon’s arrival in Atlanta; the Atlanta History Center’s photograph catalog gives 1882. Both sources are linked in Sources.

burial.text: The Historic South-View Preservation Foundation included Herndon in its neighborhood history archive.

localConnection.text: Herndon’s businesses linked him to Peachtree Street and Auburn Avenue, where he invested in commercial property. Georgia Tech’s cemetery history identified him among South-View’s residents and described his family’s connection to the cemetery. It also identified him as a member of the cemetery association’s board. His South-View connection therefore included participation in the institution as well as burial. The same account named his wives, Adrienne and Jessie, and his son, Norris, within the family’s cemetery history.

georgeunionwilder.intro: George Union Wilder escaped slavery and served in the Union Army. His South-View grave marker recorded his military service and death during the Atlanta Race Massacre.

chapters.title: Military service remembered
chapters.text: Wilder’s life began in slavery. His Union Army service is preserved on the marker at his South-View grave.

chapters.title: Brownsville and its aftermath
chapters.text: Wilder was killed in Brownsville. His grave later became a gathering place for the massacre’s centennial remembrance.

georgeunionwilder.note: Historical accounts differ on the exact date of Wilder’s death. This profile does not assign a precise day.

jeanchildsyoung.name: Jean Childs Young
jeanchildsyoung.intro: Jean Childs Young was an educator and children’s-rights advocate whose work included classroom teaching, curriculum development, and public education programs in Atlanta. She helped establish Atlanta Junior College and chaired the U.S. commission for the International Year of the Child. She also participated in civil rights activities and developed educational materials for families and teachers.

chapters.title: Education and teaching
chapters.text: Young was born in Marion, Alabama, on July 1, 1933. She studied elementary education at Manchester College and later earned a master’s degree at Queens College. She taught in Georgia and Connecticut before working in Atlanta’s elementary schools. Her work included curriculum development and teacher preparation. She also developed educational materials for families, connecting learning at home with work in the classroom. Her teaching career formed part of the educational activity that accompanied the wider civil rights movement.

chapters.title: Families and educational institutions
chapters.text: The Historic South-View Preservation Foundation described Young’s early childhood curriculum work in Atlanta Public Schools and her parent guide Bridging the Gap. Its profile also connected her with the establishment of Atlanta Junior College and support for the APEX Museum and SciTrek. These activities concerned access to education and the institutions through which children and families learned. The foundation’s account placed her work in schools alongside support for public cultural and educational organizations in Atlanta. Her educational work included support for college access and programs that introduced young people to Black history.

chapters.title: Children’s advocacy and public life
chapters.text: President Jimmy Carter appointed Young to chair the U.S. commission for the International Year of the Child in 1979. After Andrew Young’s election as Atlanta mayor, she established the Mayor’s Task Force on Public Education. In family recollections published by Canopy Atlanta, her daughter Lisa Alston described organizing around the family’s kitchen table. Alston also recalled the household’s connections with civil rights leaders and volunteers. These memories documented the domestic setting alongside Young’s work in public institutions. Young died in Atlanta in 1994.

carolyndyancey.name: Carolyn Dunbar Yancey
carolyndyancey.intro: Carolyn Dunbar Yancey was a teacher and civic leader whose work included Atlanta’s public schools and Georgia’s university system. She served on the Atlanta Board of Education and became the first Black woman appointed to the University System of Georgia’s Board of Regents. Her career connected classroom experience with public decisions about education and institutional leadership.

chapters.title: Family and education
chapters.text: Yancey was born in Detroit, Michigan, in 1921. She married physician Asa Greenwood Yancey in 1944, and the couple raised four children. The family moved to Atlanta in 1958. The Atlanta History Center’s collection guide described her educational background alongside her husband’s medical career. The collection preserved family and professional photographs. Those materials connected personal history with the educational and medical institutions in which members of the family worked in Atlanta and elsewhere. The photograph collection included images of the family home in Atlanta as well as professional events.

chapters.title: Public education and civic work
chapters.text: Yancey worked as a public school teacher before taking on educational and civic leadership roles. The Historic South-View Preservation Foundation identified her affiliations with the NAACP and League of Women Voters, along with work involving the Wesley Community Center and Spelman College. She was elected to the Atlanta Board of Education in 1982. These activities placed her in organizations concerned with public education and community affairs. Her career extended from work in classrooms into institutions that influenced educational policy and opportunities.

chapters.title: The Board of Regents
chapters.text: Governor Joe Frank Harris appointed Yancey to the University System of Georgia’s Board of Regents in 1985. The university system’s list of past regents recorded her service from 1985 to 1992. The Atlanta History Center’s collection guide identified her as the first African American woman on the board. It also described photographs of her swearing-in, preserving a visual record of that appointment. These sources linked the official record of her term with images documenting the beginning of her service to the state’s public university system.

johnlewis.name: John Robert Lewis
johnlewis.role: SNCC leader, voting-rights organizer & U.S. representative
johnlewis.intro: John Robert Lewis was a civil rights organizer and a U.S. representative from Georgia. He chaired the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee and helped lead the Selma voting-rights march attacked on Bloody Sunday. He later served on Atlanta’s city council and in Congress. His oral history connected his work in elected office with the protest movement that shaped his political life.

chapters.title: Education and student organizing
chapters.text: Lewis was born in Troy, Alabama, on February 21, 1940. He studied at American Baptist Theological Seminary in Nashville and later at Fisk University. He chaired the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee from 1963 to 1966. The committee connected student protest with organizing across the South. Lewis’s later congressional oral history described the experiences that shaped his commitment to public protest and voting rights. His account treated participation outside elected office as part of the democratic process.

chapters.title: Bloody Sunday
chapters.text: Lewis and Hosea Williams led marchers from Selma toward Montgomery to demand voting rights. After the marchers crossed the Edmund Pettus Bridge, Alabama state troopers confronted them. The troopers attacked with clubs and tear gas, and Lewis suffered a skull fracture. News coverage brought the attack before a national audience. The marchers’ demands concerned the right to register and vote without racial restrictions or intimidation. Their campaign helped build pressure for federal voting-rights legislation later that year.

chapters.title: Atlanta and Congress
chapters.text: Lewis served on Atlanta’s city council from 1982 to 1986. He entered the U.S. House on January 3, 1987, representing Georgia. He remained in Congress until his death on July 17, 2020. During his congressional career, he returned to Selma with fellow lawmakers. These visits connected the places of civil rights protest with debates over legislation and political responsibility. In his recorded interview, he discussed why he considered those returns pilgrimages and why protest continued to matter within the political process. His congressional interview also described the signing of the Voting Rights Act and his continued returns to Selma.

lillianmileslewis.name: Lillian Miles Lewis
lillianmileslewis.intro: Lillian Miles Lewis was a librarian, educator, and participant in Atlanta’s academic and civic life. She taught in Nigeria through the Peace Corps before working at Atlanta University and Clark Atlanta University. She also supported John Robert Lewis’s political campaigns. Her career included international affairs, research administration, and work with organizations concerned with education and public service.

chapters.title: Education and overseas teaching
chapters.text: Lewis was born in Los Angeles on March 3, 1939. She attended college in California and earned a master’s degree in library science at the University of Southern California. After visiting Nigeria as a student, she returned to teach through the Peace Corps. She spent two years as a volunteer teacher before returning to the United States. In 1965, she accepted a librarian’s position at Atlanta University. The move placed her within the city’s network of Black colleges and its academic and cultural life.

chapters.title: Library and civic work
chapters.text: Lewis married John Robert Lewis in 1968. The Robert W. Woodruff Library’s collection guide identified her work at Atlanta University’s Trevor Arnett Library and her service on Georgia’s State Ethics Commission. She also served as a chapter president of the National Association of Media Women. The surviving collection included correspondence, committee records, meeting minutes, reports, and materials related to librarianship. Those records documented her professional responsibilities as well as correspondence connected to her husband’s public life. The collection preserved materials relating to professional organizations and public responsibilities.

chapters.title: University administration
chapters.text: At Clark Atlanta University, Lewis served as associate director of the Institute for International Affairs and Development from 1984 to 1989. She then directed external affairs in the Office of Research and Sponsored Programs until 2003. Alongside her university work, she supported her husband’s campaigns for Atlanta’s city council and Congress. She also worked with an organization of Congressional Black Caucus members’ spouses that raised scholarship funds. These activities connected academic administration with educational and political organizations in Atlanta and Washington.

johnwdobbs.name: John Wesley Dobbs
johnwdobbs.role: Voting-rights organizer & Sweet Auburn civic leader
johnwdobbs.intro: John Wesley Dobbs worked as a railway mail clerk and organized for Black voting rights in Atlanta. He promoted voter registration through civic organizations, churches, and Masonic networks. His work helped Black Atlantans press local officials for public services and political representation. His family papers preserved evidence of that organizing alongside records of education and family life.

chapters.title: School, family, and postal work
chapters.text: Dobbs grew up in Georgia and attended school in Savannah before moving to Atlanta as a teenager. He studied at Atlanta Baptist College but left college to care for his mother. He continued his education independently. In 1903, he entered the railway mail service after passing the civil service examination. The Amistad Research Center’s family-papers guide described his Atlanta-to-Nashville mail assignment and later promotion to chief clerk. His postal work provided the professional setting for a life that also included civic organizing.

chapters.title: Family and civic networks
chapters.text: Dobbs married Irene Ophelia Thompson in 1906, and they raised six daughters. He joined the Prince Hall Masons and later became grand master in Georgia. The Amistad collection preserved correspondence, speeches, photographs, programs, and newspaper clippings documenting the family’s lives. Its description connected his Masonic leadership with work for Black suffrage and integration. The papers also recorded his concern with education and citizenship, placing civic activism alongside the family relationships that occupied his daily life.

chapters.title: Voting rights in Atlanta
chapters.text: Dobbs and attorney Austin Thomas Walden cofounded the Atlanta Negro Voters League in 1946. Dobbs pressed Mayor William Hartsfield to respond to Black voters’ demands. Atlanta hired eight Black police officers in 1948, although their authority remained restricted by segregation. Streetlights followed on Auburn Avenue. These changes showed how voting organizations pressed for services and employment within a segregated city. Dobbs continued his political work as younger activists entered the freedom struggle. He died on August 30, 1961. Dobbs promoted the ballot as a means through which Black residents could seek practical changes in Atlanta.

gracetownshamilton.name: Grace Towns Hamilton
gracetownshamilton.role: Urban League leader & pioneering Georgia legislator
gracetownshamilton.intro: Grace Towns Hamilton worked on housing, schools, health care, voting rights, and political representation in Atlanta. She led the Atlanta Urban League and later served in Georgia’s legislature. Her work included changes to Atlanta’s city charter and electoral districts. She became the first Black woman elected to the Georgia General Assembly and continued debates over representation from within public office.

chapters.title: Education and teaching
chapters.text: Hamilton was born in Atlanta on February 10, 1907. She studied at Atlanta University and earned a master’s degree in psychology at Ohio State University. She taught in Atlanta before marrying Henry Cooke Hamilton and moving to Memphis. There she taught at LeMoyne College and worked with the YWCA. She returned to Atlanta with her husband in 1941. Her early work joined teaching with research on the conditions faced by Black workers and communities. She taught psychology at Clark College and at the Atlanta School of Social Work before leaving for Memphis.

chapters.title: Urban League leadership
chapters.text: Hamilton became executive director of the Atlanta Urban League in 1943. She worked on schooling, housing, health care, and voting rights. The Atlanta History Center’s catalog described her advocacy for Black schoolchildren and voter registration. It also connected her work with construction of the Hughes Spalding Pavilion at Grady Memorial Hospital. Those efforts addressed institutions that shaped daily opportunities in segregated Atlanta. Her service at the Urban League continued until 1961, before she moved into state legislative politics.

chapters.title: Representation and city government
chapters.text: Hamilton was elected to the Georgia General Assembly in 1965. She helped develop Atlanta’s 1973 city charter, changing the balance between district and at-large representation. The Atlanta History Center identified those changes as increasing Black representation in city government. Its Boyd Lewis photograph collection preserved an image of Hamilton speaking at a senior citizens’ center, documenting public activity beyond the legislative chamber. The catalog linked that scene with her wider work on hospitals, schools, voter registration, and the rules governing local representation.

annielmcpheeters.name: Annie Lou McPheeters
annielmcpheeters.role: Librarian, historian & advocate for equal access
annielmcpheeters.intro: Annie Lou McPheeters was a librarian and educator who worked to expand access to books and Black history in Atlanta. She developed adult education programs, built the Negro History Collection, and supported library desegregation. Her career also included reference work at Georgia State College. Her work connected public reading, historical preservation, and access to professional employment.

chapters.title: Education and early library work
chapters.text: McPheeters was born Annie Lou Watters in Berwin, Georgia, on February 22, 1908. She studied English at Clark University and library science at Hampton Institute. Her early positions included teaching, school library work, and service at the Phillis Wheatley Branch in Greenville, South Carolina. She used a bookmobile to reach rural readers. In 1934, she became an assistant librarian at Atlanta’s Auburn Branch. Her early work brought her into schools and libraries operating under racial segregation.

chapters.title: Public libraries and desegregation
chapters.text: At the Auburn Branch, McPheeters developed adult education programs and established the Negro History Collection. She later took the collection to the West Hunter Branch. She worked with Black advocacy organizations that pressed for library desegregation, achieved in 1959. She joined Georgia State College as a reference librarian in 1966. In a later oral history, she discussed her career, education, and the conditions of library service in Atlanta. Her recorded recollections preserved her own perspective alongside published institutional accounts.

chapters.title: Records of civic life
chapters.text: Her papers preserved a pamphlet address by John Wesley Dobbs and a newspaper clipping about his papers.

chapters.title: Writing and historical preservation
chapters.text: McPheeters continued professional and cultural work after leaving Georgia State. She wrote about library service and Black life in Atlanta, including a memoir about her experiences in segregated and desegregating institutions. She supported the development of the Auburn Avenue Research Library. Her collection-building work helped provide the materials on which that institution was based. In May 1994, she attended the new library’s opening. She died on December 23, 1994. Her career connected the provision of books with the preservation of historical records about the readers those libraries served.

benjaminemays.name: Benjamin Elijah Mays
benjaminemays.role: Educator, minister & mentor to movement leaders
benjaminemays.intro: Benjamin Elijah Mays was a minister, scholar, and college president who opposed segregation and supported Black education. As president of Morehouse College, he taught and advised Martin Luther King Jr. He also wrote about religion and public responsibility. His career joined teaching, religious leadership, and work within institutions that educated generations of Black students.

chapters.title: Higher education and religious study
chapters.text: Mays entered Bates College in Maine in 1917 after studying in the South. He later attended the University of Chicago’s Divinity School. He interrupted his graduate studies to teach and to work with the YMCA and National Urban League, returning to complete his degrees. He earned a master’s degree in 1925 and a doctorate in 1935. During this period he entered the Baptist ministry. His academic training and teaching work developed alongside his study of African American religious life. Before leading Morehouse, he served as dean of Howard University’s School of Religion from 1934 to 1940.

chapters.title: Morehouse College
chapters.text: Mays became president of Morehouse College in 1940. His teaching and opposition to segregation influenced students, including Martin Luther King Jr. Bates College’s account of his life connected his education in Maine with his later work as a college president, minister, and civil rights mentor. It also described continuing connections between Mays and Bates, including his return visits and the institution’s later attention to his work. Those relationships placed his Morehouse presidency within a wider network of educational institutions.

chapters.title: Writing and public life
chapters.text: Mays gave the benediction at the March on Washington in 1963 and the eulogy at King’s funeral in 1968. His publications included studies of the Black church and an autobiography, Born to Rebel. The autobiography appeared in 1971 and described experiences that shaped his educational and religious work. His career also included leadership of the Atlanta Board of Education. Georgia Tech’s cemetery history identified both his Morehouse presidency and his service to the city’s public schools. He died in 1984.

horacemannbond.name: Horace Mann Bond
horacemannbond.intro: Horace Mann Bond was a historian, education researcher, and college administrator. He studied the history and unequal conditions of Black education and led Fort Valley and Lincoln universities. His research also contributed to the NAACP’s arguments against school segregation. His work connected historical scholarship with the administration of colleges and the legal struggle for equal education.

chapters.title: Education and research
chapters.text: Bond was born in Nashville, Tennessee, on November 8, 1904. He graduated from Lincoln University and pursued graduate study at the University of Chicago. Teaching and administrative work interrupted his doctoral studies. His early publications examined Black education and the economic conditions surrounding schools. His dissertation became Negro Education in Alabama: A Study in Cotton and Steel. These studies connected schooling with the agricultural and industrial systems that shaped opportunities available to Black communities. He also taught at Fisk University and served as academic dean at Dillard University.

chapters.title: College leadership
chapters.text: Bond became president of Fort Valley Normal and Industrial School in 1939. He worked on its curriculum and finances and oversaw its transition to a degree-granting college. In 1945, he became the first Black president of Lincoln University, his alma mater. He conducted research for the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund in 1953, contributing to the arguments in Brown v. Board of Education. His administrative career brought him into institutions in Georgia and Pennsylvania while he continued research on education.

chapters.title: Research records and legal work
chapters.text: Bond returned to Atlanta in 1957 to lead Atlanta University’s School of Education and later directed its Bureau of Educational and Social Research. His papers at the University of Massachusetts Amherst preserved professional and personal correspondence, research materials, teaching records, speeches, and manuscripts. The collection documented his interests in Black education and in Africa’s educational and political conditions. Its materials made it possible to follow scholarship alongside the work of managing educational institutions. The collection’s chronology also recorded his retirement in 1971 and death in Atlanta in 1972.

rubydorissmithrobinson.name: Ruby Doris Smith Robinson
rubydorissmithrobinson.role: Atlanta student activist, Freedom Rider & SNCC organizer
rubydorissmithrobinson.intro: Ruby Doris Smith Robinson was an Atlanta student activist and an organizer for the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. She joined sit-ins, the Freedom Rides, and jail-no-bail protests. She later managed resources for SNCC field organizers and became its executive secretary. Her work joined public protest with the administrative tasks that supported organizing across the South.

chapters.title: Student action and imprisonment
chapters.text: Robinson attended Spelman College and joined the Atlanta Student Movement. She participated in sit-ins and attended SNCC’s founding conference. In February 1961, she joined a jail-no-bail protest in Rock Hill, South Carolina. The participants refused to pay bail after their arrests, using imprisonment to challenge segregation. She also joined the Freedom Rides and was imprisoned at Parchman in Mississippi. These activities connected her Atlanta student organizing with campaigns elsewhere in the South. Her Freedom Ride arrest took place in Jackson, Mississippi, before her imprisonment at Parchman.

chapters.title: Organizing the Atlanta office
chapters.text: Robinson became SNCC’s administrative secretary in 1963. She coordinated support for field workers in Mississippi, Alabama, and Georgia, including their transportation needs. She helped establish the Sojourner Truth Motor Fleet as a separate organization that supplied cars for movement work. She married Clifford Robinson, who also worked with SNCC. In 1966, she became executive secretary, succeeding James Forman. The SNCC staff document preserved descriptions of work in the Atlanta office, providing organizational context for the duties carried out there.

chapters.title: A surviving cemetery record
chapters.text: A cemetery record card dated October 14, 1967, survived in the Mary Ann Smith Wilson–Ruby Doris Smith Robinson Collection on Student Activism. The Digital Library of Georgia catalog described it as a South-View record in memory of Ruby Doris Smith. The Atlanta University Center’s Robert W. Woodruff Library held the original collection. This document linked the movement organizer’s name to the cemetery through an institutional record rather than a later list of prominent residents. The catalog also identified the holding institution and collection needed to locate the original item.

bazolineeusher.name: Bazoline Estelle Usher
bazolineeusher.intro: Bazoline Estelle Usher was a teacher and administrator in Atlanta’s segregated public schools. She led schools, supervised education for Black students, and helped establish Girl Scout opportunities for Black girls. Her career included teaching at Spelman College after retirement from the public schools. She also recorded recollections of education, community life, and Atlanta University in an oral history.

chapters.title: Teaching and school leadership
chapters.text: Usher returned to Atlanta to teach in 1915 after working in Virginia. She held teaching and leadership positions at Wesley Avenue Grammar School, Booker T. Washington High School, and David T. Howard Grammar School. The Atlanta History Center’s collection guide described her progression from classroom teaching to school administration. It also identified her graduate study at Atlanta University. Her work took place in a school system that separated Black and white students, limiting the institutions and resources available to Black children.

chapters.title: Schools and Girl Scouts
chapters.text: Usher helped bring Girl Scouting to Black girls in Atlanta in 1943, working with Grace Towns Hamilton. The following year she became director and supervisor of the city’s African American schools. The Atlanta History Center’s guide connected her administrative work with the opening of elementary schools. It also described her election to the local Girl Scout board and her later teaching at Spelman College. These activities extended educational work beyond the classroom into youth organizations and the training of future educators.

chapters.title: An account in her own voice
chapters.text: Usher recorded an oral history with interviewer E. Bernard West on December 19, 1979. In it, she discussed her education and social life at Atlanta University, her teaching and administrative career, and memories of W. E. B. Du Bois. The interview also included her recollections of the Atlanta Race Massacre. The Atlanta History Center preserved the recording within its Living Atlanta oral history collection. The catalog connected the interview to the city’s schools and to places in Walton County, providing a record of how her educational career was remembered.

The Historic South-View Preservation Foundation also included Usher in its neighborhood archive. A Georgia Historic Preservation Division article described her educational work, while the Atlanta History Center preserved photographs related to her family and school career. ludieclayandrews.name: Ludie Clay Andrews
ludieclayandrews.role: Nurse educator & advocate for equal professional rights
ludieclayandrews.intro: Ludie Clay Andrews was a nurse educator who challenged restrictions on Black nurses’ professional registration in Georgia. She organized nurse training in Atlanta and worked to secure access to the same licensing examination taken by white nurses. Her career connected hospital care, professional education, and opposition to racial exclusion in the institutions that governed nursing employment.

chapters.title: Training and nursing education
chapters.text: Andrews was born in Milledgeville, Georgia, in 1872. She attended Eddy High School and graduated from the nursing program at MacVicar Hospital at Spelman Seminary in 1906. She later organized the Municipal Training School for Colored Nurses at Grady Memorial Hospital. The Georgia Public Library Service’s nursing history identified the school’s establishment in 1914 and its charter in 1917. The training program operated within a profession whose schools, licensing practices, and employment opportunities were shaped by racial segregation. The program trained Black nurses for professional practice.

chapters.title: Access to professional registration
chapters.text: Andrews pressed for Black nursing graduates to take the state’s registration examination. Georgia Women of Achievement described her refusal of an individual license offered without equivalent access for other qualified Black nurses. She instead pursued changes that would apply to graduates more broadly. In 1920, Black graduates of accredited nursing schools in Georgia gained access to the same state examination as white graduates. Andrews became Georgia’s first Black registered nurse. Her campaign linked her own professional standing with opportunities for the nurses she trained.

chapters.title: Hospital leadership and later recognition
chapters.text: Andrews continued hospital work in Atlanta, including leadership at the infirmary serving Morehouse, Spelman, and Atlanta University. Georgia Women of Achievement described her service in public health and community organizations alongside her nursing responsibilities. She retired from active nursing work in 1948. Morehouse School of Medicine’s nursing-program history later identified her as an influence on its emphasis on health justice and professional education. That institutional account connected her training work at Grady with the struggle for equal examination rights in Georgia.
